passages.t: ‘God is known in Judah’: the weapons broken
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments. A Psalm of Asaph. A song” (verse 1). The song opens: “God is known in Judah; His name is great in Israel” (verse 1). “His tent is in Salem, His dwelling place in Zion” (verse 2).

There, at his own city, God broke the weapons of war. “There He shattered the flaming arrows, the shield and sword and weapons of war” (verse 3). The bravest soldiers fell asleep for the last time (verse 5). “At Your rebuke, O God of Jacob, both horse and rider lie stunned” (verse 6).

Then the psalm widens. God judged from heaven, and the earth went quiet, “when God rose up to judge, to save all the lowly of the earth” (verse 9). Even human anger will end up giving God praise (verse 10).

It closes with a call. Keep the promises you made to God (verse 11). He is feared by the kings of the earth (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Salem is an old name for Jerusalem. In Genesis, Melchizedek is “king of Salem” (Genesis 14:18). The name sounds like shalom, the Hebrew word for peace. So the city of peace is where God breaks the weapons of war.

The psalm names no battle. Many readers connect it with the night the Assyrian army fell back from Jerusalem in King Hezekiah's day, when “Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and withdrew” (2 Kings 19:36). Others read it as a song for worship that celebrates God's rule over Zion again and again, with no one battle in mind. Both readings are held.

‘Horse and rider’ (verse 6) would ring a bell for any Israelite. It is the phrase of Moses' song at the Red Sea: “The horse and rider He has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:1). Chariots were the most feared weapon of the day. In Israel's songs they are no match for God.

Notice who God rises to save: ‘all the lowly of the earth’ (verse 9). His judging is for the weak, not only for one nation.
passages.later:
Isaiah saw a day when the nations “will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks” (Isaiah 2:4). Psalm 76 sings of God breaking weapons; Isaiah sees people beating them into farm tools.

Jesus said, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God” (Matthew 5:9). And Revelation names the risen Jesus “KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS” (Revelation 19:16), the one before whom the rulers of the earth must bow.
passages.asks:
What weapons are you trusting, and which ones are aimed at you? Psalm 76 says that God is stronger than both. It does not hand his victory to any modern army or nation. It gives it to God, and to the lowly he rises to save.

Verse 11 also asks something plain. Have you made a promise to God in a hard time? Keep it now that the time has passed.
